extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants drafting or prosecuting computer-implemented inventions (Canada)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing patentability, sufficiency, utility, and claim drafting for computer-implemented inventions under the Canadian Patent Act and Patent Rules. Covers subject-matter categories, contribution analysis, divisional applications, disclosure requirements, and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application properness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application (the “original application”) describes more than one invention, an applicant may file a divisional application to protect described inventions other than the one invention only to which the original application’s claims were directed or, as the case may be, to which the original application’s claims were limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the content of the specification and drawings of the purported divisional to the parent to determine if the divisional's claims are directed to a different invention and whether the divisional was filed with new matter. If claims are not directed to a different invention than the parent, the later-filed application is not a proper divisional under section 36. If a divisional has a presentation date after Oct 30, 2019 and contains new matter relative to its parent, it is defective under sections 91 or 155.7 of the Patent Rules. If a divisional was 'directed by the Patent Office', double-patenting does not apply between the divisional and parent/siblings. Amendments introducing new matter are governed by subsection 38.2(3.1) of the Patent Act or 155.6 of the Patent Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must fall within statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed subject-matter of a computer-implemented invention must fall within one of the five categories in the section 2 definition of 'invention': art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance refines how those five categories apply to computer-implemented inventions (e.g., methods as art; devices as machines; physical memory storing instructions as manufacture). Certain items (computer programs per se, data structures, computer-generated signals) may not be statutory. See related chapters for finer distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method (art) criterion: solution to a practical technological problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A method that, on its own merits, would be considered non-statutory does not become statutory simply by virtue of some part of the method being carried out on or by a computer. The method itself, as a whole, must be a solution to a practical problem and must lie within a field of technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A method of controlling a computer’s operations so as to achieve a technological result would come within the definition of invention. In such methods, the electronic processes are considered to include at least one act performed by a physical agent upon a physical object, producing a change of condition. Claims to game-playing or creating works of art typically do not define inventions that belong to a field of technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process criterion: must apply a statutory method
rubrics_metrics.description: A process implies the application of a method to a material or materials. To be statutory, a process must apply a statutory method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing contribution of a computer-implemented process, consider that necessary ingenuity can arise from the method, from the material(s), or from the recognition that applying the method to the material leads to an unexpected useful result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine/device criterion: must provide a technological solution (contributed practical form)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim to a device to be patentable it must define at least one statutory element that forms part of the contribution. The device itself must be a contributed practical form providing a novel and unobvious technological solution to a technological problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination can be by assessing the device itself or indirectly by reference to the method implemented. A machine adapted to implement a patentable method is necessarily a solution to a practical problem. The technological solution need not be an improvement to the computer as a general purpose device; adapting a general purpose device to act as a special purpose device suffices. Examples include known hardware controlled by new software or new arrangements of known hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability not negated by software-based adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a device provides a technological solution, its patentability does not depend on whether it was adapted by providing new hardware or by controlling existing hardware in a particular manner by the addition of software or firmware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether adaptation is via hardware or software, assess novelty and inventiveness of the contribution. Software-programmed adaptations can render a machine patentable if they provide a novel and inventive technological solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objecting to claims defined by discrete non-statutory features
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a device does not provide a solution to a technological problem, and is further defined in terms of discrete non-statutory features, the claim would be objected to on the ground that it does not define a statutory 'invention' within section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A computer cannot be patentably distinguished from other computers simply on the basis of stored information; stored information does not cause the computer to become a new and unobvious solution to a practical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture category and physical medium storage
rubrics_metrics.description: The category manufacture applies where a computer is used to control a manufacturing process, or where a non-machine computer product is claimed. The concept of a non-machine computer product applies to a physical memory storing computer-executable instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A computer program per se is not statutory because it is disembodied; a physical medium storing the program may be considered a manufacture. Patentability of such products depends on the nature of the contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must include a statutory contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable claim must include a statutory contribution. For a claim directed to a computer, it must be determined whether the device itself is part of the contribution — i.e., whether the computer itself may be considered novel and inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the essential elements of the device that, as a set, provide a technological solution to a technological problem. That set must be novel and inventive. If a machine implements a non-statutory method, inventive ingenuity associated with the method does not provide the inventive step necessary for the machine; the inventive effort must relate to adapting the machine to implement the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment when only part of method is on the computer
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where the computer only implements part of a patentable method, care must be taken to base the assessment only on those parts of the method which take place on the computer, and not on the basis of the method as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus contribution analysis on the computerized steps; do not attribute inventiveness from non-computer steps to the computer-implemented portion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between program design and code expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing a computer program (developing a method, flow charts, design diagrams or pseudocode) can involve inventive effort; expressing a computer program in a specific programming language (writing code) is considered to fall within the common general knowledge of an uninventive skilled programmer and is not considered to require inventive effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive ingenuity necessary to provide patentability to a computer is never found simply in writing computer code to express a developed program. Thus, the presence of source code in an application is not, by itself, indicative of inventive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer program per se and when it bestows patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer program is not, by itself, statutory subject-matter. However, if the result of running the program on a computer provides a novel and inventive technological solution to a technological problem, then the program is viewed as modifying the technological nature of the computer as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the program expresses a statutory method that is novel and inventive, the programmed computer would be patentable. If the program expresses a non-statutory method, the non-statutory method itself is not a patentable contribution, regardless of novelty. Patentability of computer claims in such cases will depend on additional elements defining how the computer is adapted to implement the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution analysis guided by the description (technical problem and solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 56(1)(d) of the Patent Rules states that 'a description of the invention must be set out in terms that permit the technical problem and its solution to be understood, even if that problem is not expressly stated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should be clear from the description what technical (technological) problem is being addressed and what solution is being proposed. The level of detail in the description is informative when considering whether ingenuity was required in implementation. Lack of details about how the computer performs operations suggests the applicant considers the manner uninventive and may indicate no invention in the reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility: usefulness, demonstrable or by sound prediction, operable and reproducible
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be useful in the sense of doing whatever was promised by the inventors. The utility of the claimed subject-matter must be established by demonstration or sound prediction, and must be operable to produce the promised result in a manner that is controllable and reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computers are generally capable of reproducibly performing operations, but the invention as a whole may require other elements for proper operation. If operator judgement/interpretative reasoning is implicated in proper operation, reproducibility may not be satisfied. Where an operator's input is required but involves no judgement, reproducibility is not affected. When claiming computer-implemented methods, it must be unambiguously clear which steps are carried out on/by a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency: written description and enablement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must correctly and fully describe the invention (written description) and provide any teachings necessary to allow a person skilled in the art to operate the claimed invention (enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A skilled person must understand, from the specification alone and common general knowledge, what the invention is, what it does, and how to make it work. Level of description depends on facts: known elements can be merely identified; novel applications of hardware/software require greater detail. Where claimed as means-plus-function, the nature and arrangement of the means must be clear. Limited description may indicate the applicant believes suitable means are readily apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm and flowchart disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-implemented inventions often rely on algorithms or logic trees; where these lie at the heart of the invention, a full description of the algorithm or logic tree should be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flow charts should be accompanied by a written explanation. To enable practice of the invention, the skilled person must be able to put each step of the flowchart into operation without recourse to inventive ingenuity or undue experimentation. The amount of written description necessary depends on which steps are part of common general knowledge; if certain steps would not be obvious to the skilled person, those operations must be fully described. If common general knowledge would lead to inoperative attempts, the description should include instructions to avoid inoperative embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source code vs pseudocode in disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Source code or pseudocode may be provided, but will generally not be considered by themselves to provide a full and enabling description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source code's significance may depend on the intended platform and may not be a clear and unambiguous description. Pseudocode, being a semi-structured natural language explanation, usually has greater value than source code for describing the functioning of an intended program because it does not depend on a specific programming language's syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples as guidance for contribution/novelty assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Worked examples illustrate application of contribution analysis, showing how to treat information-only claims, storage-media claims, computer-implemented methods, systems, and claims that amount to mental methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate: (a) information (atomic coordinates) as non-statutory by form; (b) storage medium statutory in form but lacking contribution if medium known; (c) methods that implement technological steps may be statutory but require inventive step over prior art; (d) systems/machines specifically adapted to perform patentable methods inherit patentability if adapted; (e) claims that merely define intellectual content or mental steps executed on a computer may be defective under section 2. Use examples to guide whether features are mere information, mental methods, or technological contributions.
